items.stem: A toy car is sitting still. What must happen for it to start moving?

options.text: Someone gives it a push or a pull
options.rationale: Correct: a still object needs a force (a push or pull) to start moving.

options.text: It will move on its own after a while
options.rationale: Objects at rest stay still until a force acts on them.

options.text: It only moves if it is red
options.rationale: Colour has nothing to do with movement.

options.text: It needs to be switched on
options.rationale: A simple toy car with no motor just needs a push or pull.

items.explanation: Correct: a still object needs a force (a push or pull) to start moving.
items.domain_ref: Pushes and pulls all around us
items.provenance: original Mastemy item drafted by an AI agent; no external question source

items.stem: Which TWO of these are pulls? (Select TWO.)

options.rationale: Correct: you pull the drawer towards you.

options.text: Tugging a wagon by its handle
options.rationale: Correct: tugging the handle is a pull.

options.text: Kicking a football away from you
options.rationale: Kicking pushes the ball away, so it is a push.
Pressing is a push, not a pull.

items.explanation: Correct: you pull the drawer towards you.

items.stem: You roll the same ball on a carpet and on a smooth floor with the same gentle push. Where does it stop sooner?

options.text: On the carpet, because the rough surface slows it down
options.rationale: Correct: rougher surfaces create more friction and slow the ball sooner.
The smooth floor lets the ball roll further, so it stops later.

options.text: They always stop at exactly the same place
options.rationale: The surface changes how far the ball rolls.

options.text: The ball never stops on carpet
options.rationale: The ball does stop; friction slows it down.

items.explanation: Correct: rougher surfaces create more friction and slow the ball sooner.
